messages.subject: Warning message: Strange genotype pattern.
messages.body_plain:
I'm working with a family of offspring from two wild parents, and as I didn't have phase information or genetic distances (only physical), I have used the LinkMFEX package. This analyses the male and female mapping parent separately to calculate map distances, and gives most probable phase for each linkage group, with alleles coded as A or H for the female parent data set and B or H for the male parent.

Now when I enter these into R/qtl, the female data set is interpreted as a backcross
 (Genotypes (%):      AA:55.0  AB:45.0)
and the male set as an F2 intercross
 (Genotypes (%):      AA:0.0  AB:43.1  BB:56.9  not BB:0.0  not AA:0.0)
with the message (for the male only): strange genotype pattern.

So is this allele coding not correctly interpreted by R/qtl? And why might the two data sets (from the same offspring) behave differently? Thanks for any advice!

messages.body_plain:
Hi there -
Ripple is only a really good way to order markers if a) you already have a good general idea of the marker order (e.g. physical positions), or b) you only have a few markers. Since ripple is a local algorithm, if you have lots of markers, it can get stuck in the order you input and not find the optimal order.

There are a lot of options to generate linkage maps - joinmap is the most popular, you could also use ASMap::mstmap. I am pretty sure joinMap can handle your cross type... not sure about ASMap. If you don't own JoinMap and ASMap doesn't do the trick, another option is to use a travelling salesperson problem solver to order markers based on recombination fractions. This approach is implemented in qtlTools::tspOrder. To use tspOrder, you'll need to install qtlTools from github...

> library(devtools)
> install_github("jtlovell/qtlTools")
> library(qtlTools)

You'll also need to download and install the Concorde travelling salesperson problem solver. Instructions for how to do this are in the help file ?tspOrder.
John

messages.subject_clean: LOD threshold and p value for considering the qtl significant
messages.body_plain:
You can permutate LOD scores across the genome for scanone and scantwo function to establish a threshold based on a given false discovery rate. I do not see why P-value < 0.63 would make any sense. Also, P-value from which test? If you fit a multiple QTL model and calculate an ANOVA table using a drop-one-term analysis, you will get a P-value associated with the F-statistic that says something about the increase in the fit of the full model by adding a given QTL. it is common to use a stringent cut-off for this, 0.01 or lower. P-values for t-tests for the hypothesis that the effect size > 0 should probably be considered significant if p < 0.05. The LOD score of a single QTL should be considered significant if it is higher than 95% of the permutated genome-wide (ie "no QTL" NULL model) LOD scores. The multiple QTL model uses a penalized LOD score threshold.  Hope this helps.

messages.subject_clean: QTL significant in scanone, but not in multiple QTL models
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I am not sure how to interpret my finding for a minor QTL peak on linkage group 4 in the scanone, which is no longer significant after including covariates (composite interval mapping or multiple QTL model; see fig LODcurvesLG4.pdf). It seems to be that when added as a pair, the major QTL on LG2 cancels out the minor QTL on LG4 (see figure scantwo.pdf). This surprises me, as this is usually the case that after accounting for the variation associated with a major QTL, you will INCREASE the power to detect additional, small effect QTL. Here it seems to be reversed. The effect of these QTL is in the same direction (all QTL have effects in the same direction in this cross), so they are not repulsing QTL

Additional information of interest: this is a QTL scan in one of two mapping populations (families) of the same interspecies cross (n=94). The other family (n=136) has the same QTL on LG4 that is only significant in scanone, but not in multiple QTL models. Combining the two family-specific maps (n=230) and performing a QTL scan gives significant QTL on LG4 in both scanone and fitqtl output.

Figure legends:

LODcurves show the LOD scores along LG4 from scanone (dashed line is 5% significance cut-off), CIM, and fitqtl after accounting for the effects from major QTL on LG1 and LG2 (significance thresholds for CIM and fitqtl are very close to the dashed line).

scantwo shows the increase in LOD score when adding two QTL as a pair allowing for epistasis (lower triangle) or only allowing for additive effects (upper triangle) relative to a single QTL model. Notice that QTL on LG1 and LG4 together approach significance, but that a pair of QTL on LG2 and LG4 does not.

I would be interested to hear any suggestions as to how to interpret this result.

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] switch.order abuse?
messages.body_plain:
If you ensure that the two crosses have the same markers in the same order, you could use ripple() on a given chromosome with each cross, and then sum either the LOD scores of the crossover counts.

  rip1 <- ripple(cross1, method="countxo", chr=3, window=7)
  rip2 <- ripple(cross2, method="countxo", chr=3, window=7)
  rip <- rip1
  rip[,"obligXO"] <- rip1[,"obligXO"] + rip2[,"obligXO"]
  summary(rip)

or for the likelihood method:

  rip1 <- ripple(cross1, method="likelihood", chr=3, window=4)
  rip2 <- ripple(cross2, method="likelihood", chr=3, window=4)
  rip <- rip1
  rip[,"LOD"] <- rip1[,"LOD"] + rip2[,"LOD"]
  summary(rip)

Alternatively, if you're willing to assume that the recombination rates are the same in the two crosses, you could combine your two 4-way cross objects into one and build the map using the two crosses combined.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Using controlAcrossCol=TRUE (or alpha/n_pheno) would both be seeking to control the overall family-wise error rate: if none of the expression phenotypes are affected by a QTL, have just 5% chance of any of them showing significant results. You'll need a *lot* more permutations, maybe on the order of **16 million**, because you have to go way out into the tail of the marginal distributions.

The results you're getting suggest that >50% of the time, at least one of the 16k phenotypes has a LOD score that is above the 99.9% quantile of its marginal null distribution.

You could try doing FDR across the expression traits, as you'd mentioned in your first paragraph: get the p-value of the biggest LOD score for each of the 16k traits, and then turn those into q-values, for example with the bioconductor package qvalue.

karl

The issue of selecting a pair of very tightly linked QTL won't go away completely by clipping off the individuals' with extreme genotypes. So rather than omitting individuals, I'd be inclined to just drop the pair of QTL from the model, if you think they are an artifact.

And rather than look at the phenotype vs genotype distribution at each individual marker, I'd want to look at the phenotypes broken up into the 9 possible two-locus genotypes. I'd expect that one of the recombinant classes has one or a few individuals with high or low phenotypes.

Regarding your second question: the % var explained in the drop-one-QTL table is a transformation of the LOD score comparing the model with all of the QTL to the model with that one QTL dropped. The % var explained from the full model is a transformation of the LOD score comparing the full model with all QTL to the model with no QTL. They overall % var generally won't be equal to the sum of the individual values. And results in the drop-one-QTL table are really only meaningful in the case of unlinked QTL.

messages.body_plain:
The pairs of very tightly linked QTL that I see are generally QTL linked in repulsion, with effects of opposite sign. And I'd think they're either both real or both artifacts, so I wouldn't exclude one but rather both.

The key thing to look at, in deciding whether the QTL can be trusted or not, is the recombinant individuals. And I'd want to have at least two markers between them. If there are just one or two animals that have different genotypes at the two QTL, definitely think artifact. If there are 5-10 or more recombinant individuals, I'd be much more confident about the QTL.

It's hard to put a distance threshold on this, because it depends on the sample size. If you have 1000 individuals, you can more confidently identify tightly linked QTL, than if you have just 100 individuals.

karl

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

In one of my data set, I got a major QTL with large effect size and high Lod score. The position of the peak is consistent using scanone, CIM or scantwo. This position also corroborates with results from other intercrosses. However, after I used refineqtl in multiple QTL models, either with or without other minor QTL in the model, the position of this peak shifted about 1 cM, causing the marker closest to the peak to shift one over. This may sound like nit-picking as the change is small but I want to understand what could have cause the shift of the peak location. Also in this case, which location do we have more confidence on? What signs would you look for to make the decision?

Some more information: there is no missing data for any individual on this linkage group but I still tried increasing rounds of simulation. Not surprisingly, it had no effect on the refineqtl result.

Thank you very much!
